readings.c1s1:
¶
'''whip-socket''' (hwip′sok″et), ''n.'' A socket attached to the dashboard of a vehicle, to receive the butt of the whip.

'''whip-staff''' (hwip′ståf), ''n.'' '''1.''' A whiphandle.—'''2.''' ''Naut.'', a bar by which the rudder is turned: an old name for the ''tiller'' in small vessels. ''Falconer.''

'''whip-stalk''' (hwip′stâk), ''n.'' Same as ''whip-stock.''

'''whipster''' (hwip′stėr), ''n.'' [< ''whip'' + ''-ster.''] '''1.''' Same as ''whipper-snapper.''
{{smaller block|Every puny ''whipster'' gets my sword.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2. 244.}}
That young liquorish ''whipster'' Heartfree.
{{right|''Vanbrugh'', Provoked Wife, v. 3.}}}}
'''2†.''' A sharper. ''Bailey'', 1731.

'''whip-stick''' (hwip′stik), ''n.'' Same as ''whip-stock.'' {{smaller|—'''Whip-stick palm.''' See ''palm''<sup>2</sup>.}}

'''whip-stitch''' (hwip′stich), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To sew over and over: especially used in bookbinding. Compare ''whip, v. t.'', 4.—'''2.''' In ''agri.'', to half-plow or rafter. ''Imp. Dict.'' [Local, Eng.]

'''whip-stitch''' (hwip′stich), ''n.'' [< ''whip-stitch, v.''] '''1.''' In ''agri.'', a sort of half-plowing, otherwise called ''raftering.'' [Local, Eng.]—'''2.''' A hasty composition. ''Dryden.'' [Rare.]—'''3.''' A particle; the smallest piece. [Colloq.]—'''4.''' A tailor: used in contempt.

'''whip-stitching''' (hwip′stich″ing), ''n.'' See ''whipping'', 4.

'''whip-stock''' (hwip′stok), ''n.'' The staff, rod, or handle to which the lash of a whip is secured. Also ''whip-stalk, whip-stick.''
{{smaller block|Out, carter;
Hence, dirty ''whipstock''; hence, you foul clown.}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''whirlblast''' (hwėrl′blȧst), ''n.'' A whirling blast of wind; a whirlwind.
{{smaller block|The ''whirl-blast'' comes, the desert sands rise up.
{{right|''Coleridge'', Night-Scene.}}
<poem>A ''whirl-blast'' from behind the hill
Rushed o’er the wood with startling sound.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Poems of Fancy, iii.}}
<poem>Were this bitter ''whirl-blast'' fanged with flame,
To me ’twere summer, we being side by side.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Paolo to Francesca.}}}}

'''whirlbone''' (hwėrl′bōn), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''whyrlebone''; < ME. ''whirlbon'', ''whyrlebone'', ''whorlebone'' (= MD. ''wervelben''); < ''whirl'' + ''bone''<sup>1</sup>. Hence, by confusion, ''hurlbone''.] '''1†.''' The bone of a ball-and-socket joint, as in the hip.
{{smaller block|The . . . ''whirlebones'' of their hips, about which their hucklebones turne. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xxviii. 11.}}}}
'''2.''' The patella; the kneepan or stifle-bone.
{{smaller block|''Patella.'' . . . La palette du genouil. The ''whirlebone'' of the knee. {{right|''Nomenclator.'' (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''whirler''' (hwėr′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''whirl'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who or that which whirls.—'''2.''' In ''rope-manuf.'', one of the revolving hooks to which the hemp is fastened in the operations of twisting it into rope-yarn or small rope.

'''whirl-fire†''' (hwėrl′fīr), ''n.'' Lightning.
{{smaller block|<poem>The smoaking storms, the ''whirl-fire’s'' crackling clash,
And deafening Thunders.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Lawe.}}}}

'''whirlgig''' (hwėrl′gig), ''n.'' Same as ''whirligig'', 4.

'''whirlicote†''' (hwėr′li-kōt), ''n.'' [Appar. for ''whirlcote'' (cf. ''whirligig'' for ''whirlgig''), < ''whirl'' + ''cote''<sup>1</sup>.] A wheel-carriage.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|whip-socket|6904|whirl-pillar}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''whip-socket''' (hwip′sok″et), ''n.'' A socket attached to the dashboard of a vehicle, to receive the butt of the whip.

'''whip-staff''' (hwip′ståf), ''n.'' '''1.''' A whiphandle.—'''2.''' ''Naut.'', a bar by which the rudder is turned: an old name for the ''tiller'' in small vessels.   ''Falconer.''

'''whip-stalk''' (hwip′stâk), ''n.'' Same as ''whip-stock.''

'''whipster''' (hwip′stėr), ''n.''   [< ''whip'' + ''-ster.'']   '''1.''' Same as ''whipper-snapper.''
{{smaller block|Every puny ''whipster'' gets my sword.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2. 244.}}}}
{{smaller block|That young liquorish ''whipster'' Heartfree.
{{right|''Vanbrugh'', Provoked Wife, v. 3.}}}}
'''2†.''' A sharper.   ''Bailey'', 1731.

'''whip-stick''' (hwip′stik), ''n.'' Same as ''whip-stock.'' {{smaller|—'''Whip-stick palm.''' See ''palm''<sup>2</sup>.}}

'''whip-stitch''' (hwip′stich), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To sew over and over: especially used in bookbinding. Compare ''whip, v. t.'', 4.—'''2.''' In ''agri.'', to half-plow or rafter.   ''Imp. Dict.'' [Local, Eng.]

'''whip-stitch''' (hwip′stich), ''n.''   [< ''whip-stitch, v.'']   '''1.''' In ''agri.'', a sort of half-plowing, otherwise called ''raftering.'' [Local, Eng.]—'''2.''' A hasty composition.   ''Dryden.'' [Rare.]—'''3.''' A particle; the smallest piece. [Colloq.]—'''4.''' A tailor: used in contempt.

'''whip-stitching''' (hwip′stich″ing), ''n.'' See ''whipping'', 4.

'''whip-stock''' (hwip′stok), ''n.'' The staff, rod, or handle to which the lash of a whip is secured. Also ''whip-stalk, whip-stick.''
{{smaller block|Out, carter;
Hence, dirty ''whipstock''; hence, you foul clown. Be gone.
{{right|''T. Tomkis'' (?), Albumazar, iv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Phoebus, when
He broke his ''whipstock'', and exclaim’d against
The horses of the sun.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Two Noble Kinsmen, i. 2.}}}}

'''whip-tail, whip-tailed''' (hwip′tāl, -tāld), ''a.'' Having a long, slender tail like a whip-lash: as, the ''whip-tail'' scorpion. See ''whip-scorpion.''

'''whip-tom-kelly''' (hwip′tom-kel′i), ''n.'' The black-whiskered vireo or greenlet of Cuba, the Bahamas, and Florida, ''Vireo barbatulus:'' so called in imitation of its note. {{smaller|It closely resembles the common red-eyed vireo of the United States, but has black mystacial stripes. Compare cut under ''greenlet.''}}

'''whip-top''' (hwip′top), ''n.'' A top which is spun by whipping. Also ''whipping-top.''
{{smaller block|We have hitherto been speaking of the ''whip-top;'' for the peg-top, I believe, must be ranked among the modern inventions, and probably originated from the te-totums and whirligigs. {{right|''Strutt'', Sports and Pastimes, p. 492.}}}}

'''whip-worm''' (hwip′wėrm), ''n.'' A nematoid parasitic worm, ''Trichocephalus dispar'', or another of this genus, as ''T. affinis'', the cæcum-worm of sheep. {{smaller|They have a long, slender anterior part and a short, stout posterior part, like a whip-lash joined to a whip-stock.}}

'''whir''' (hwėr), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''whirred'', ppr. ''whirring.''   [Also ''whirr'', and formerly ''whur;'' prob. < Dan. ''hvirre'', whirl, twirl, = Sw. dial. ''hwirra'', whirl; cf. G. ''schwirren'', whir, buzz. Cf. ''whirl.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To fly, dart, revolve, or otherwise move quickly with a whizzing or buzzing sound; whizz.
{{smaller block|When the stone sprung back again, and smote}}
<poem>Earth, like a whirlwind, gath’ring dust with ''whirring'' fiercely round,
For fervour of his unspent strength, in settling on the ground.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xiv. 343.}}}}
<poem>The lark
''Whirred'' from among the fern beneath our feet.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', The Borderers, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The blue blaze ''whirred'' up the chimney and flashed into the room.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|And the ''whirring'' sail [of the windmill] goes round.
{{right|''Tennyson'', The Owl, i.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To hurry away with a whizzing sound.
{{smaller block|<poem>This world to me is like a lasting storm,
''Whirring'' me from my friends.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, iv. 1. 21.}}}}

'''whir''' (hwėr), ''n.''   [Also ''whirr''; < ''whir'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The buzzing or whirring sound made by a quickly revolving wheel, a partridge’s wings, etc.
{{smaller block|As my lord’s brougham drives up, . . . the ladies, who know the ''whirr'' of the wheels, and may be quarreling in the drawing-room, call a truce to the fight.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, iv.}}}}
'''2†.''' A turn; commotion.
{{smaller block|They flapt the door full in my face, and gave me such a ''whurr'' here.
{{right|''Vanbrugh'', Journey to London, ii. 1.}}}}

'''whirl''' (hwėrl), ''v.''   [Formerly also ''wherl'', ''whurl''; < ME. ''whirlen'', ''whwirllen'', ''wirlen'', contr. from *''whervelen'' = MD. ''wervelen'', whirl, = G. ''wirbeln'', whirl, = Icel. ''hvirfla'' = Sw. ''hvirfla'' = Dan. ''hvirvle'', whirl; freq. of the verb represented by AS. ''hweorfan'', etc., turn: see ''wherve'', and cf. ''warble''<sup>1</sup>. The E. verb is perhaps due to the Scand.; it depends in part on the noun.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To swing or turn rapidly round; rotate, or cause to revolve rapidly.
{{smaller block|A-bowte cho ''whirllide'' a whele with her whitte hondez.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3261.}}}}
{{smaller block|My thoughts are ''whirled'' like a potter’s wheel.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., i. 5. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|With that his faulchion he ''wherled'' about.
{{right|''Robin Hood and the Stranger'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 416).}}}}
'''2.''' To cast with a twirling or twisting motion; throw with a rapid whirl.
{{smaller block|And proudest Turrets to the ground hath ''whurld.''
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|First Sarpedon ''whirl’d'' his weighty lance.
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xvi. 585.}}}}
'''3.''' To carry swiftly away with or as if with a revolving or wheeling motion.
{{smaller block|<poem>See, see the chariot, and those rushing wheels,
That ''whirl’d'' the Prophet up at Chebar flood.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', The Passion, l. 37.}}}}
{{smaller block|The last red leaf is ''whirl’d'' away.
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xv.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Uplifted by the blast, and ''whirled''
Along the highway of the world.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Golden Legend, ii.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|To twirl, spin, revolve, rotate.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To turn rapidly; move round with velocity; revolve or rotate swiftly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Four [moons] fixed, and the fifth did ''whirl'' about
The other four.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 2. 183.}}}}
{{smaller block|This slippery globe of life ''whirls'' of itself.
{{right|''Lowell'', Parting of the Ways.}}}}
'''2.''' To pass or move with a rapid whirling motion, or as if on wheels. {{smaller block|<poem>I’ll come and be thy waggoner,
And ''whirl'' along with thee about the globe.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., v. 2. 49.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>What thoughts of horror and madness ''whirl''
Through the burning brain.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Mogg Megone, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|The supply of material in the world is practically constant; nothing drops off of it as we ''whirl'' through space, and the only thing added is some stray meteorite, insignificant except in the way of a sign or wonder.
{{right|''Jour. Franklin Inst.'', CXXX. 88.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Whirling chair''', an apparatus formerly used to subdue intractable patients in retreats for the insane. After the victim had been strapped in, the chair was made to revolve very rapidly.—'''Whirling dervish.''' See ''dervish.''—'''Whirling plant.''' Same as ''telegraph-plant.''}}

'''whirl''' (hwėrl), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whirl'' (in comp.) = MD. ''wervel, worvel,'' a whirl, peg, a spinning-wheel, = OHG. ''wirbil, wirfil,'' a whirlwind, MHG. G. ''wirbel,'' a whirl, the crown of the head, = Icel. ''hvirfill,'' a circle, ring, the crown of the head: see ''whirl, v.,'' and cf. ''wharl''<sup>1</sup>, ''whorl.'']   '''1†.''' The whorl of a spindle.
{{smaller block|A ''whirle'', . . . a round Piece of Wood put on the spindle of a spinning-wheel. {{right|''Bailey'', 1731.}}}}
{{smaller block|Medle you with your spyndle and your ''whirle.''
{{right|''Udall'', Roister Doister, i. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' A reel or hook used in rope-making for twisting strands of hemp or gut.—'''3.''' A rope-winch. —'''4.''' In ''bot.'' and ''conch.'' See ''whorl.''—'''5.''' A rapid circling motion or movement, as that of a revolving body; rapid rotation, gyration, or circumvolution: literally and figuratively: as, the ''whirl'' of a top or of a wheel; the ''whirls'' of fancy.
{{smaller block|Thus I would prove the vicissitudes and ''whirl'' of pleasures about and again. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now with sprightly
Wheel downward come they into fresher skies; . . .
Still downward with capacious ''whirl'' they glide.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Sleep and Poetry.}}}}
'''6.''' Something that whirls, or moves with a rapid circling motion; the circling eddy of a whirlpool, a whirlwind, or the like.
{{smaller block|<poem>What flaws, and ''whirls'' of weather,
Or rather storms, have been aloft these three days!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Pilgrim, iii. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon the ''whirl'', where sank the ship,
The boat spun round and round.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', Ancient Mariner, vii.}}}}

'''whirl-about''' (hwėrl′a-bout″), ''n.'' '''1.''' Something that whirls with velocity; a whirligig.—'''2†.''' A great fish of the whale kind; a whirl-whale.
{{smaller block|<poem>The monstrous ''Whirl-about'',
Which in the Sea another Sea doth spout,
Where-with huge Vessels (if they happen nigh)
Are over-whelm’d and sunken suddenly.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 5.}}}}

'''whirlbat''' (hwėrl′bat), ''n.''   [Also, by confusion, ''hurlbat''; < ''whirl'' + ''bat''<sup>1</sup>.]   The ancient cestus, a kind of boxing-glove used by Greek and Roman athletes. See cuts under ''cestus''<sup>1</sup>, 2
{{smaller block|<poem>Your shoulders must not undergo the churlish ''whoorlbat’s'' fall;
Wrastling is past you, strife in darts, the foot’s celerity;
Harsh age in his years fetters you, and honour sets you free.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xxiii. 538.}}}}
{{smaller block|He rejected them, as Dares did the ''whirlbats'' of Eryx, when they were thrown before him by Entellus.
{{right|''Dryden'', Pref. to Fables.}}}}

'''whirlblast''' (hwėrl′blȧst), ''n.'' A whirling blast of wind; a whirlwind.
{{smaller block|The ''whirl-blast'' comes, the desert sands rise up.
{{right|''Coleridge'', Night-Scene.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A ''whirl-blast'' from behind the hill
Rushed o’er the wood with startling sound.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Poems of Fancy, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Were this bitter ''whirl-blast'' fanged with flame,
To me ’twere summer, we being side by side.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Paolo to Francesca.}}}}

'''whirlbone''' (hwėrl′bōn), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''whyrlebone''; < ME. ''whirlbon'', ''whyrlebone'', ''whorlebone'' (= MD. ''wervelben''); < ''whirl'' + ''bone''<sup>1</sup>. Hence, by confusion, ''hurlbone''.]   '''1†.''' The bone of a ball-and-socket joint, as in the hip.
{{smaller block|The . . . ''whirlebones'' of their hips, about which their hucklebones turne. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xxviii. 11.}}}}
'''2.''' The patella; the kneepan or stifle-bone.
{{smaller block|''Patella.'' . . . La palette du genouil. The ''whirlebone'' of the knee. {{right|''Nomenclator.'' (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''whirler''' (hwėr′lėr), ''n.''   [< ''whirl'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who or that which whirls.—'''2.''' In ''rope-manuf.'', one of the revolving hooks to which the hemp is fastened in the operations of twisting it into rope-yarn or small rope.

'''whirl-fire†''' (hwėrl′fīr), ''n.'' Lightning.
{{smaller block|<poem>The smoaking storms, the ''whirl-fire’s'' crackling clash,
And deafening Thunders.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Lawe.}}}}

'''whirlgig''' (hwėrl′gig), ''n.'' Same as ''whirligig'', 4.

'''whirlicote†''' (hwėr′li-kōt), ''n.''   [Appar. for ''whirlcote'' (cf. ''whirligig'' for ''whirlgig''), < ''whirl'' + ''cote''<sup>1</sup>.]   A wheel-carriage.

{{smaller block|Of old time, Coaches were not known in this Iland, but Chariots or ''Whirlicotes'', then so called, and they onely used for Princes or great Estates, such as had their footmen about them. {{right|''Stow'', Survey of London (ed. 1633), p. 70.}}}}
'''whirligig''' (hwėr′li-gig), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Early mod. E. ''whirlygig'', ''whyrlygigge''; also ''whirlgig'' (in def. 4, with a var. ''whirlwig''); < ME. ''whyrlegyge''; < ''whirl'' + ''gig''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' Any toy or trivial object to which a rapid whirling motion is imparted. {{smaller|Especially—(''a'') A tee-totum, or a top.}}
{{smaller block|I tryll a ''whirlygig'' rounde aboute. Je pirouette. . . . I holde the a peny that I wyll tryll my ''whirlygig'' longer about than thou shalte do thyne. {{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 762.}}}}
{{smaller block|Hath the truth been hid in corners, that we must grope for it in a sectary’s budget? Or are not such men rather sick of Donatism? That every novelist with a ''whirligig'' in his brain must broach new opinions!
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 180.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
They [the gods] gave Things their Beginning,
And set this ''Whirligig'' a Spinning. ''Prior'', The Ladle.
</poem>}}
{{smaller|(''b'') A toy which children spin in the hand by means of string. (''c'') A carrousel or merry-go-round. (''d'') A toy resembling a miniature windmill, which children cause to spin or whirl round by moving it through the air.}} '''2.''' Hence, anything that revolves or spins like a whirligig; also, spinning rotation; revolving or recurring course.
{{smaller block|The ''whirligig'' of time brings in his revenges.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., v. 1. 385.}}}} '''3.''' In ''milit. antiq.'', an instrument for punishing petty offenders, as a kind of wooden cage turning on a pivot, in which the offender was whirled round with great velocity.—'''4.''' In ''entom.'', any one of numerous species of water-beetles of the family ''Gyrinidæ'', as ''Gyrinus natator'', usually seen in large numbers on the surface of the water, circling rapidly about, and diving only to escape danger. {{smaller|When caught, many exude a milky liquid having an odor of apples. They abound in fresh-water ponds, pools, and ditches. The larvæ are aquatic, and breathe by means of ciliate branchiæ. The American whirligigs belong to the genera ''Gyrinus'', ''Dineutus'', and ''Gyretes''. See cut under ''Gyrinidæ''. Also ''whirlgig'', ''whirlwig'', and ''whirlwig-beetle''.}}

'''II.†''' ''a.'' Whirling.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thrise to her bed sliding shee quayls, with ''whirlygig'' eyesight
Up to the sky staring.</poem>
{{right|''Stanihurst'', Æneid, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|And so continuing their ''whirlegigg''-deuotions with continuall turnings.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 307.}}}}

'''whirling-table, whirling-machine''' (hwėr′ling-tā″bl, -mạ-shēn″), ''n.'' '''1.''' A machine contrived for the purpose of exhibiting the principal effects of centripetal or centrifugal forces, when bodies revolve in the circumferences of circles or on an axis.—'''2.''' In ''pottery'', a potters’ lathe for holding a plaster mold in which is laid a thin mass of clay, to form a plate or other circular piece. {{smaller|The mold shapes the inside of the piece, and a templet approached to the revolving mold forms the outside. See ''potters’ wheel'', under ''potter''<sup>1</sup>.}} '''3.''' A horizontal arm mounted for rotation about a vertical axis, used in experiments in aërodynamics, in determining the constants of anemometers, or for other purposes for which high velocities are desired under conditions thus attainable.

'''whirl-pillar''' (hwėrl′pil″ä̤r), ''n.'' A waterspout; a dust-whirl.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
